strengths: Addresses a practical and under-explored problem: fine-grained, font-controllable text editing for poster design, where preserving typographic style and layout is critical.
Proposes a dual-stream visual conditioning mechanism using reference glyph patches and a VLM-based OCR model, enabling multi-region editing without font labels at inference.

Conducts extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks, including an in-house poster benchmark, AnyText, IAM, and CVL, with quantitative and qualitative comparisons against recent commercial and open-source models.
Reports strong gains on the AnyText benchmark in text fidelity and distributional metrics, e.g., English Sen. Acc. 85.36% and FID 6.12, outperforming FLUX-Text and AnyText2.
Demonstrates generalization to handwritten text-line generation without handwritten-specific training, achieving competitive HWD scores (1.32 on IAM, 0.89 on CVL).
Includes ablation studies on Font Style Reference and the text-region weighted loss, supporting the design choices.
Provides useful qualitative comparisons in Figures 4-6 across English, Chinese, and handwritten styles.
weaknesses: A central method detail is missing: the glyph reference map X_glyph is described as target text rendered in the reference font, but the manuscript does not explain how this is obtained from a user-provided cropped glyph patch. This makes the pipeline difficult to reproduce and weakens the claim that no font labels or font files are needed.
The in-house SkyReels-Text benchmark is only 200 samples and is not public; the 100k training dataset and code are not released, severely limiting reproducibility and independent verification.

The paper overstates state-of-the-art performance: in Table 1, FLUX-Text achieves better B-PSNR (34.53 vs. 34.17), and in Table 3 on CVL, DiffBrush achieves a better GS (29.6 vs. 31.0, if lower is better). The abstract and conclusion nevertheless claim state-of-the-art visual realism.

There is no human/user study or designer evaluation, which is important for a poster-design application. The DINO similarity metric is not a validated measure of fine typographic style and may miss glyph-level differences.

The VLM-based OCR model is used for data curation, verification, and likely inference, but its accuracy is not quantitatively evaluated. Using the same OCR for data filtering and verification risks circularity and bias toward fonts it can already recognize.
Table 2 uses an undefined 'Baseline' method, and the table caption lacks details about what baseline is and how FID/LPIPS are computed for text editing, making the comparison less transparent.

The ablation on the loss weight λ shows small differences between λ=5 and λ=10, and the choice of λ=5 is not supported by statistical tests or confidence intervals. No error bars or significance testing are reported overall.

The technical novelty is limited: the method largely combines existing components—Qwen-Image-Edit with LoRA, frozen VAE feature concatenation, a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL OCR, and DMD2 distillation—without a fundamentally new architecture or training paradigm.
Potential ethical/legal issues around collecting real-world posters and fonts from design platforms are not discussed, and there is no limitations or failure-case analysis.

strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem—fine-grained, font-controllable text editing for poster design—with clear relevance to real design workflows, where semantic correctness and typographic fidelity must be jointly preserved.

The proposed conditioning mechanism is user-friendly: it requires no font labels or per-font fine-tuning at inference, letting users supply cropped glyph patches as explicit visual references for style transfer, which is a sensible and flexible interface for professional typography.

The empirical results are strong and reasonably consistent across several evaluations: the in-house SkyReels-Text benchmark (Table 1), the AnyText English/Chinese benchmark (Table 2), and handwritten datasets IAM/CVL (Table 3), often outperforming both specialized and general/commercial editing models.

The ablation studies (Table 4) are informative: they isolate the contribution of the Font Style Reference (FSR) module and justify the choice of the text-region loss weight (λ = 5), showing the expected trade-off between text fidelity and background preservation.

The method generalizes beyond its training distribution—it handles multilingual content and even handwritten text lines without handwriting-specific training, which is a meaningful demonstration of transfer capability.

The DMD2 distillation to an 8-step student model (≈10× speedup) improves practical deployability without materially degrading font-controllable editing quality, which matters for an interactive design tool.
Qualitative comparisons (Figures 4–6) visually support the quantitative claims, showing better preservation of reference typography and background structure than several strong baselines.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited. The core ingredients—LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen-Image-Edit, concatenation of frozen-VAE features for dual-stream conditioning, a spatially reweighted diffusion loss, and DMD2 distillation—are largely off-the-shelf, and the main contribution is best characterized as a carefully engineered pipeline rather than a new technical principle.

The headline benchmark (SkyReels-Text benchmark, 200 samples) is curated in-house, and its construction, annotation protocol, and inter-annotator reliability are not adequately described. This makes the reported 'state-of-the-art' claims in Table 1 harder to verify independently and raises a possible bias concern.

The training data generation pipeline depends on other models (Qwen3-8B for divergent text replacement and an editing model for content replacement), so errors can propagate into the training set. The two-pronged verification (VLM OCR + DINO similarity) is only a partial safeguard, and DINO similarity is a weak proxy for true font identity.

Some experimental comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples. In Table 1 the compared baselines (e.g., Nano Banana, Seedream 4.0, FLUX-Kontext-Pro, Qwen-Image-Edit) are general editing models that are not designed for glyph-reference conditioning, and the inputs/settings differ; the 'Baseline' row in Table 2 is left undefined, which is a clarity/reproducibility gap.

For a design-oriented application, no perceptual or user study involving designers is reported. Font fidelity is assessed mainly through DINO similarity and OCR-based metrics, which do not fully capture typographic correctness or aesthetic intent.

The paper reports no failure cases, limitations, or error analysis, and some qualitative results (e.g., the 'FRESH'/'A.P.C.' example in Figure 4) show imperfect font transfer, suggesting the method is not uniformly reliable on highly stylized or ornamented fonts.

Reproducibility is constrained: training consumed substantial compute (≈512 A100-hours for the editor and ≈72 A100-hours for the VLM OCR) and depends on a large curated poster dataset that is not clearly released, and the exact architecture modifications for injecting the dual-stream features are only briefly specified.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely useful and underexplored problem: fine-grained, font-controllable text editing for poster/design workflows, where existing general-purpose editors (FLUX-Kontext, Qwen-Image-Edit, Seedream, Nano Banana) demonstrably fail to preserve or transplant typography. The task formulation (per-region content + reference glyph conditioning) is clean and clearly stated.

The data-curation pipeline is thoughtfully designed. The content-style decoupling strategy (generating semantically disjoint replacement text with Qwen3-8B, editing to preserve typography, then verifying with both a VLM-OCR re-check and DINO feature similarity) directly attacks a real failure mode of synthetic text-editing datasets, and the critique of prior synthetic data (limited font diversity, unrealistic backgrounds, unnatural glyph-background integration) is well-argued.

The empirical coverage is broad for a single paper: an in-house poster benchmark, the AnyText benchmark in English and Chinese, and handwritten benchmarks (IAM, CVL), plus ablations on the Font Style Reference module and the text-region loss weight λ. Figures 1, 2, 4, 5, and 6 are informative and qualitatively convincing, spanning Latin and CJK text, single and multi-region layouts.

The demonstrated generalization to handwritten text generation without any handwriting-specific training is a notable and somewhat surprising result (HWD 1.32/0.89 on IAM/CVL, competitive with dedicated methods such as DiffBrush and One-DM).
The writing is generally clear, the method diagram (Fig. 3) communicates the dual-stream conditioning well, and the training/inference setup (LoRA rank, batch size, LR, GPU-hours) is reported.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty relative to the claim of a 'novel font-controllable framework.' The core mechanism amounts to concatenating frozen-VAE features of (i) an inpainted reference poster and (ii) a rendered glyph image onto the noise latent of Qwen-Image-Edit, which is then LoRA-fine-tuned. This is essentially inpainting plus glyph-image conditioning, closely related to prior glyph-conditioned editors (AnyText, TextDiffuser, GlyphDraw, GlyphControl, FLUX-Text) and to reference-image-conditioned editing models. No controlled experiment isolates the benefit of this specific conditioning design against simpler alternatives (ControlNet, embedding injection, or routing the glyph patch through the VLM branch).

Evaluation circularity is a material concern. The authors fine-tune a Qwen2.5-VL-based OCR model, then use it to curate training data, verify generated pairs, and compute the primary evaluation metrics (Sentence Accuracy, NED, Spatial IoU). The paper's own discussion of Table 4 concedes that this OCR 'struggle[s] to accurately parse highly stylized or ornate text produced when FSR is enabled' — i.e., the accuracy metric is unreliable precisely in the stylized regime the method targets. Accuracy numbers may therefore be biased in favor of the authors' own outputs.

Font/style fidelity — the paper's central claim — is measured mainly by DINO similarity between generated and reference text regions. DINO features are a coarse proxy for typographic identity (stroke terminals, serifs, weight, slant, ligatures, letterform proportions). No human/user study is reported, despite this being a design-oriented task where perceptual judgment is the ultimate criterion.

Benchmarking is hard to interpret. Headline comparisons against commercial systems (Nano Banana, Seedream 4.0, FLUX-Kontext-Pro, Qwen-Image-Edit) are made on a 200-sample in-house benchmark curated by the authors, which naturally favors the proposed method; the benchmark is not described as publicly released. On the public AnyText benchmark the accuracy gains over FLUX-Text are marginal (Sen. Acc. 85.36 vs 84.19; NED 0.9406 vs 0.9400), with the real advantage confined to FID/LPIPS. The 'Baseline' row in Table 2 is never defined, and the improvement over it (0.8292 → 0.8536 Sen. Acc.) is small.

The headline capability of simultaneous multi-region editing with heterogeneous typographic styles is not quantitatively evaluated in the main text — the paper explicitly defers multi-font results to the appendix, and the main figures show single-font edits. A claim of this prominence should be supported by a dedicated quantitative experiment and failure analysis.

Several claims are asserted without supporting evidence. The 'over 10× speedup in inference' from DMD2 distillation has no latency measurement, no student-vs-teacher quality comparison, and no ablation. Similarly, the claim that SkyReels-Text 'establishes a new SoTA' rests largely on the self-curated benchmark, and the claim of 'zero-shot font transfer without additional parameters' is questionable given LoRA fine-tuning on in-domain data plus added VAE-conditioning channels.

A core practical question is left unaddressed: what happens when the target text contains characters absent from the reference glyph patch? This is the common case in real poster edits (e.g., changing a slogan, as in Fig. 4 where 'REVOLUTION' supplies the style for 'FOREVER INNOVATIVE'). The paper provides no coverage study, no failure-case analysis, and no discussion of how far style extrapolation extends.

Reproducibility is limited. The pipeline depends on several large models (Qwen2.5-VL-7B fine-tuned, Qwen3-8B, Qwen-Image-Edit, DINOv2) and a two-stage training cost of roughly 512 + 72 A100-hours; the 100k-sample curated dataset and the in-house benchmark are not stated to be released. This makes independent verification of the central data-curation contribution effectively impossible.

Minor but real inconsistencies: in Table 1 the proposed method's B-PSNR (34.17) is worse than FLUX-Text (34.53), yet background preservation is described as 'comparable'; in Table 3 the CVL IS score (1.71) is essentially tied with DiffBrush (1.70), which is presented as superior; and Table 4 shows FSR degrades text accuracy (0.9327 → 0.8334), a trade-off that is explained away rather than analyzed.

strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem: font-controllable text editing for professional poster/design workflows, where fine-grained typographic control is genuinely needed but underserved by general-purpose editors.

Introduces a reasonable dual-stream visual conditioning scheme that explicitly decouples content (plain-text reference) and style (rendered glyph map) and injects both into the MMDiT backbone via a frozen VAE, avoiding font labels and test-time fine-tuning.

Evaluation is broad and multi-faceted: scene text (AnyText, English/Chinese), handwritten text (IAM, CVL), small-size and paragraph-level editing, multi-font editing, plus a user preference study, with consistent SOTA numbers across Tables 1–3.

Valuable data contributions: an expert-annotated SkyReels-OCR-40K dataset and a 100K content-style decoupled dataset with a two-pronged (OCR NED + DINO v2) verification strategy; these are documented in detail in the supplement.

Ablations on the Font Style Reference and the text-region weighted loss (Table 4), including a λ sweep, give insight into the design choices, and the DMD2 distillation enables practical 8-step inference (~8s).

The paper is clearly written and organized, with strong qualitative figures (e.g., Figures 4, 6, 12, 14, 15) illustrating behavior across languages, fonts, and difficulty levels; code and models are promised to be released.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate. The core is a LoRA fine-tune of Qwen-Image-Edit with standard latent concatenation of VAE-encoded conditions and a masked weighted reconstruction loss; most components (SAM2 masks, DINO verification, DMD2 distillation, ControlNet-style conditioning) are off-the-shelf, so the advance is largely an integration/engineering effort rather than a new mechanism.

Training data is synthesized by commercial/foundation models (Nano Banana for editing, Qwen3-8B for divergent text, SAM2 for masking). The approach therefore risks distilling a stronger teacher (Gemini 2.5 Flash) rather than establishing a fundamentally new capability, and the paper does not analyze how much of the gain is attributable to the teacher's signal versus the proposed conditioning.

The plain-text reference X_text is itself produced by inpainting the masked text region with the target text, i.e., it is a model-generated intermediate. This introduces potential error propagation and circularity, and the paper does not quantify the sensitivity of the final result to the quality of X_text or provide a clean ablation isolating this factor.

Part of the evaluation is self-referential: the SkyReels-Text benchmark is in-house and Sen.Acc/NED are computed with the authors' own fine-tuned OCR, which is the same model used to construct/validate the training data. This weakens the independence of the headline numbers, even though AnyText/IAM/CVL provide some external grounding.

The ablation is somewhat counter-intuitive and under-explained: without the Font Style Reference, Sen.Acc (0.9327) and NED (0.9734) are higher than with it (0.8334/0.9502). The stated reason (the task becomes simpler, and the OCR struggles on stylized text) suggests the metrics may not cleanly capture the intended capability, and this deserves deeper analysis rather than a brief justification.

The 'zero-shot' framing is overstated. The model is fine-tuned on a large, in-domain 100K dataset built specifically for this task, so it is test-time-finetuning-free rather than zero-shot in the usual sense; the abstract/introduction should state this precisely.

Limited discussion of failure cases and limitations beyond a brief mention of paragraph-level artistic styles; quantitative failure analysis (e.g., when reference glyphs are ambiguous or backgrounds are complex) is largely absent.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant problem—font-controllable text editing for poster design—with a clean formulation: regional text replacement conditioned on user-provided glyph patches, requiring neither font labels nor test-time fine-tuning.

The dual-stream visual conditioning design (plain-text reference image plus glyph map, encoded by a frozen VAE and concatenated with the noisy latent) is simple and effective; the ablation in Table 4 supports its value, with the Font Style Reference notably improving Spatial IoU (0.6986→0.7506) and DINO (0.6995→0.8503).

The data pipeline is a substantive contribution: a fine-tuned VLM OCR (Qwen2.5-VL 7B) for ornamental/calligraphic text, a content–style decoupling strategy using an LLM for divergent text, a strong editor for style-preserving replacement, and two-pronged verification via OCR-NED and DINOv2 similarity, yielding a documented 100K paired dataset.

Empirical validation is broad and consistent: an in-house 200-sample benchmark, AnyText (English/Chinese), IAM/CVL handwritten benchmarks, a 4-way user preference study, and ablations. Results are strong across settings (e.g., AnyText English Sen. Acc 0.8536 and FID 6.12 vs. 13.85 for FLUX-Text; best HWD on IAM 1.32 and CVL 0.89).

Demonstrated practical capabilities beyond single-font editing: simultaneous multi-font-region editing in one pass, zero-shot generalization to handwritten text without dedicated training, small-text editing down to ~20 px, and paragraph-level editing, with DMD2 distillation giving an 8-step (~10× faster) inference path.

The paper is generally clear and well-organized, with informative qualitative figures (Fig. 4, 5, 6, 14, 15) and a reasonably thorough related-work discussion of both general image editing and specialized text editing models.
weaknesses: Baseline fairness is under-specified for a paper whose central claim is font control. It is not stated whether multi-image-capable baselines (e.g., Qwen-Image-Edit, Seedream 4.0, FLUX-Kontext-Pro) were provided the reference glyph image as an additional input. The only note is that FLUX Pro cannot take multiple references and is omitted, which suggests baselines generally did not receive the style reference. This asymmetry should be made explicit and, where possible, a reference-conditioned baseline should be included.

Potential metric circularity/confound: the in-house benchmark's Sen. Acc and NED are computed with the authors' own fine-tuned VLM OCR. The FSR ablation is a red flag—removing the style reference yields higher content accuracy (Sen. Acc 0.9327 vs. 0.8334), which is explained away as the OCR struggling with stylized text. If the automatic metric is unreliable precisely on the highly stylized text this method targets, the headline numbers in Table 1 are partly confounded. A human content-accuracy evaluation on the same samples would materially strengthen the claims.

Technical novelty of the core mechanism is moderate: concatenating VAE-encoded reference latents with the noisy latent and LoRA-tuning a Qwen-Image-Edit/DiT backbone with a region-weighted diffusion loss and DMD2 distillation is largely a recombination of existing components. The main originality lies in the task framing, the conditioning-by-glyph-patch interface, and the data curation, rather than the model architecture.

Coverage of closest competitors in the primary table is incomplete: Table 1 omits TextCtrl, AnyText, and AnyText2, which are the most directly comparable style/text-editing methods (they appear only in Table 2 on AnyText). FID/LPIPS are also not reported on the in-house benchmark, limiting assessment of visual realism there.

Reproducibility constraints: the abstract promises code and models, but the curated dataset and the in-house benchmark (200 samples) are not clearly committed to release; the data-generation pipeline depends on proprietary models (e.g., Nano Banana/Gemini). The OCR annotation protocol (10 experts) lacks inter-annotator agreement, and training costs (512 + 72 A100-hours) make reproduction non-trivial.

The abstract's claim of state-of-the-art in 'both text fidelity and visual realism' is slightly overstated: on the in-house benchmark the method's B-PSNR (34.17) is below FLUX-Text (34.53), and the content-accuracy metric is confounded as noted above.

Limitations are thinly discussed: there is no failure-case analysis, little discussion of scripts beyond English/Chinese (vertical text, RTL, perspective/3D scene text in real photographs), and the acknowledged weakness on paragraph-level artistic styles is relegated to the supplementary. A dedicated limitations section would improve the paper.

strengths: Well-motivated and practically relevant task: fine-grained, reference-glyph-driven text editing for poster design is genuinely under-served by existing scene-text editors and general image editors, and the formulation (user-supplied cropped glyph patch + target text + region) is clean and directly useful for professional workflows.

Substantial data-centric contributions: SkyReels-OCR-40K (≈40K images, 10 domain experts, MUSIQ/NRQM/Q-Align filtering) and a 100K content-style-decoupled pair dataset with a two-pronged verification gate (NED ≥ 0.9 and DINO v2 ≥ 0.8). If released, these could be useful resources.

Empirical coverage is broad on paper: in-house benchmark, AnyText (English/Chinese), IAM and CVL, plus ablations, qualitative comparisons and a user study. Baselines include a reasonable mix of open-source (FLUX-Text, AnyText, AnyText2, TextCtrl, Calligrapher, DiffSTE, DiffUTE, TextDiffuser) and commercial systems (Nano Banana, Seedream 4.0, FLUX-Kontext-Pro).

Zero-shot-style generalization to handwritten text (Table 3, Tables 7–8) without dedicated handwriting fine-tuning is a nice qualitative demonstration, and the multi-font single-pass editing in Figure 15 is a practically valuable capability.

The dual-stream conditioning mechanism (VAE-encoded plain-text reference + glyph map concatenated with the noisy latent, plus a text-region-weighted loss and DMD2 distillation) is conceptually simple and easy to implement, which lowers adoption cost.
weaknesses: Evaluation circularity: the text-accuracy metrics (Sen. Acc, NED) in Sec. 4.3 are computed with the authors' own fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL OCR model, which is itself part of the data-filtering pipeline (Sec. 3.2). The same model that gates the training data is also the judge of the model's outputs, and Table 6 shows this OCR outperforming Qwen3-VL-8B on a benchmark authored by the same team. The main quantitative claims therefore rest on a self-referential measurement loop.

The central ablation contradicts the paper's own headline claim. Table 4 shows that disabling FSR (the paper's main contribution) *increases* Sen. Acc (0.9327 vs. 0.8334) and NED (0.9734 vs. 0.9502). The authors dismiss this by arguing their own OCR 'struggles to parse highly stylized text,' which is a post-hoc rationalization rather than an explanation, and it directly undermines the claim of simultaneous gains in semantic accuracy and typographic fidelity.

The gap over the Qwen-Image-Edit baseline is implausibly large (Table 2: FID 35.62 → 6.12 English, 19.26 → 5.44 Chinese; LPIPS 0.2499 → 0.0246). Such a drop is far more consistent with a metric-computation artifact or with training-set overlap with the evaluation data than with a conditioning-mechanism change. Both AnyText and SkyReels-OCR draw on AnyWord-3M / LAION / Wukong, yet contamination risk is never discussed. The in-house 200-sample benchmark (Sec. 4.2) is likewise ambiguous about whether it is disjoint from the curated training pool.

Critical ablations are missing. The paper's core claim is the *dual-stream* conditioning, but only a binary FSR on/off and λ are ablated; there is no ablation of the plain-text reference stream alone, the glyph stream alone, the VLM instruction stream, the DMD2 distillation, or the data scale. Without these, the large gains over baseline cannot be attributed to the proposed method rather than to the 100K in-domain fine-tuning pairs.

The λ ablation is essentially noise. λ=5 and λ=10 differ by 0.0003 in Spatial IoU and 0.0001 in DINO, yet the paper concludes λ=5 is 'the optimal balance.' This does not establish robustness of the loss design.

Potentially unfair baseline comparison. The reference-font training targets are generated by Nano Banana (Sec. 3.2, Fig. 2), and Nano Banana is then treated as a competitor in Table 1 and Fig. 4. Comparisons to proprietary models lack version/date, prompt-selection protocol, and number of attempts, making the win rates in Fig. 7 and the quantitative rankings hard to interpret.
The user study (Fig. 7) reports win rates without participant count, recruitment, task instructions, interface, or significance testing, so it cannot substantiate the strong human-preference claim.

Reproducibility is thin. The abstract promises 'Code and models are publicly available at' but the URL is truncated in the PDF; no release plan is given for SkyReels-OCR-40K or the 100K decoupled dataset, and the pipeline depends on proprietary models (Nano Banana, Seedream) plus scraped Pinterest/Amazon imagery with unclear licensing.

The 'zero-shot' handwritten claim is not fully supported: Sec. 3.2 states SkyReels-OCR covers 'handwritten, calligraphic, printed, and customized artistic fonts,' and AnyWord-3M also contains handwriting styles, so the assertion that the model is 'not explicitly trained on handwritten data' is questionable.

Limited technical novelty. VAE-encoded conditioning concatenated with the latent, a text-region-weighted reconstruction loss, and DMD2 distillation are all individually known; the 'dual-stream visual conditioning' reduces to feature concatenation plus LoRA on an off-the-shelf Qwen-Image-Edit backbone. No new architectural or training insight is introduced.

Presentation gaps in the main text: no limitations section, no failure cases, and no inference-cost comparison against baselines (only a passing '~8 seconds on a single A800 GPU' buried in the supplement). The SOTA claim in the abstract rests primarily on a 200-sample in-house benchmark with self-trained metrics.
